query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) engineered by incorporating higher levels of passivating elements (such as Al and Cr) will form robust and self-healing oxide films at high temperature and under mechanical wear, leading to significantly superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance compared to conventional structural alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional structural alloys that suffer rapid degradation under combined high-temperature and tribo-corrosion conditions due to inadequate or unstable protective oxide layers.
generation.intervention: Alter the alloy composition by using multiple principal elements—including passivating species like Al and Cr—to produce a high-entropy alloy designed to rapidly develop and regenerate a protective oxide layer during operation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures combined with mechanical wear (tribological stress) in corrosive environments (e.g., molten salts or high oxidative atmospheres).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and sustained presence of a continuous, robust, self-healing oxide film (such as alumina and/or chromia) on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The high configurational entropy of the HEA and the targeted incorporation of passivating alloying elements promote rapid in situ formation of protective oxide/passivation films. These films act as diffusion barriers that reduce the exposure of the base metal to both corrosive species and wear, thus limiting degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA is expected to exhibit a notably lower tribo-corrosion rate (e.g., reduced material loss or thickness reduction) under harsh thermal and mechanical conditions compared to conventional structural alloys.
generation.baseline: Performance of conventional structural alloys lacking such optimized, self-healing oxide layer formation, which typically show higher degradation rates under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: While the overall trend of improved degradation resistance is expected, the magnitude of improvement will depend on the specific concentrations of passivating elements, microstructural factors, and exact operating conditions. There is uncertainty in the precise quantitative improvement until tested.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal element ratios and the quantitative extent of degradation resistance improvement remain uncertain and require systematic experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of HEAs with variable concentrations of passivating elements (e.g., different Al and Cr levels) and a conventional alloy control sample. Subject all samples to a high-temperature tribological testing regime in a corrosive environment (such as molten salt or a simulated oxidative atmosphere under applied wear load). Monitor the evolution, integrity, and protective effectiveness of the oxide films as well as overall degradation rates.
measurements: Surface analysis for oxide film formation and composition (using XPS, SEM-EDS, or similar methods)
Weight loss or thickness reduction measurements over time
Tribological performance metrics (e.g., coefficient of friction and wear track profiling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEAs with enhanced passivating element content do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in maintaining a protective oxide layer and exhibit similar or greater tribo-corrosion degradation rates compared to conventional alloys, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. frame.system: Structural alloys used in extreme environments that suffer accelerated degradation from the combined effects of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion. The focus here is on recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) that include multiple principal elements compared to traditional single‐ or dual‐element alloys.
frame.goal: Achieving superior resistance to tribo-corrosion degradation under extreme operating conditions such as high temperature and mechanical wear.
frame.limitation: Conventional structural alloys degrade rapidly under the simultaneous effects of wear (tribology) and corrosion at high temperatures, which limits their reliability and lifetime in extreme environments.
constraints: exposure to coupled mechanical (tribological) and chemical (corrosive) stress
need for improved long-term durability over currently used alloys
frame.regime: Extreme service conditions that combine high temperature with wear-induced corrosion (tribo-corrosion) regimes.
prior_attempts: Use of traditional structural alloys which have proven inadequate under such harsh conditions due to their inability to sustain protective surface films and mechanical integrity during simultaneous wear and corrosion.

families.principle: Altering the elemental makeup to exploit high entropy effects, thereby enabling the formation of robust, self-healing oxide/passivation films that maintain stability at elevated temperatures and resist tribo-corrosion.
cues_for: superior degradation resistance versus conventional alloys
families.best_lever: Incorporation of elements (e.g., Al, Cr or other refractory/passivating species) that promote stable, protective oxide film formation under harsh, high-temperature and wear-corrosion conditions.

families.principle: Modifying the surface or interface—via coatings or in-situ passivation—to provide an extra barrier against wear-corrosion and to help sustain protective films even under aggressive conditions.
cues_for: conventional alloys degrade partly due to an inability to sustain protective surface films
cues_against: the focus is on bulk HEAs and their intrinsic superior resistance, rather than separate coating strategies
families.best_lever: Leveraging alloying-induced in-situ formation of ultra-thin, self-healing passivating oxide layers at the surface to mitigate film degradation under simultaneous mechanical and chemical attack.

families.principle: Designing the internal microstructural layout (grain size, phase distribution, interfaces) to modulate mechanical integrity and passivation characteristics, thereby reducing degradation during wear and corrosion.
cues_against: no explicit mention of engineered microstructure but rather material composition cues dominate the question
families.best_lever: Tailoring a bimodal or dual-phase microstructure with refined grains that balance mechanical strength and chemical passivity under extreme conditions.

families.principle: Using tailored heat treatments or thermo-mechanical processes to adjust grain size and phase stability, thus potentially enhancing high-temperature oxidation and wear resistance.
cues_for: need to sustain protective films under harsh conditions
cues_against: the primary emphasis is on the intrinsic ability of the HEA’s composition to resist tribo-corrosion, rather than processing-induced microstructural changes
families.best_lever: Optimized annealing or thermomechanical protocols that improve oxide scale adherence and refine the microstructure for better performance at high temperatures.

families.principle: Adjusting synthesis/fabrication parameters to control chemical homogeneity and phase distributions that could indirectly affect resistance to high-temperature tribo-corrosion.
cues_for: recent developments in alloy systems might benefit from novel processing
cues_against: the question emphasizes material composition (HEAs) rather than processing techniques
families.best_lever: Employing advanced casting or powder metallurgy methods to achieve homogenous phase distribution, though this lever is secondary given the composition focus.
